_readme: Hand-labelled routing evaluation set (SPEC section 11, Stage 2). `expected_tier` is a human judgement of the cheapest tier that could answer acceptably -- it is NOT what any router produced. The set is deliberately weighted towards cases where prompt length and prompt difficulty come apart, because that is exactly what the naive token-count rule cannot see. Categories prefixed `trap_` are the ones designed to fail.

prompts.prompt: Here is my diary entry from last Tuesday. I woke up at about half past six in the morning, which is earlier than usual for me, and the light was already coming through the curtains in that thin grey way it does in early spring. I made coffee in the little steel pot my sister gave me two Christmases ago, and I stood in the kitchen drinking it while the radio talked about the weather and a council meeting about a new bus lane. My neighbour's dog was barking at something in the garden, probably the same cat as always. I answered a few emails that had come in overnight, none of them urgent, mostly people confirming things that had already been confirmed. Around nine I walked to the shop on the corner to buy bread and milk, and the woman behind the counter mentioned that her son had got into the university he wanted, which was nice to hear. On the way back I noticed the crocuses were finally out along the wall by the church. I spent most of the middle of the day working on the spreadsheet for the quarterly report, which was tedious but not difficult, and I broke for lunch around one and ate the leftover soup from Sunday. In the afternoon I had a call with the team that ran long, mostly because we kept circling the same point about scheduling without anyone quite deciding anything. Afterwards I went for a walk along the canal to clear my head, and the light was very good, low and gold on the water. I got back around six, cooked pasta, watched two episodes of something forgettable, and went to bed at about eleven. My question is simple: what day of the week was the day described in this entry?

Below is the full text of an email thread from my colleagues about the office move. Hi all, just confirming that the move is going ahead on the fifteenth as planned. Please have your desks cleared by the evening of the fourteenth. Thanks, Priya. Reply from Marcus: Noted, thanks Priya. Will the meeting rooms on the third floor be available on the sixteenth or should we book externally? Reply from Priya: They should be, but I will confirm with facilities tomorrow. Reply from Devon: Can I ask whether the new office has bike storage? I cycle in most days and it would change my commute quite a bit if not. Reply from Priya: Yes, there is a secure bike room in the basement, and there are showers on the ground floor. Reply from Marcus: One more thing, will the standing desks be moved or are we getting new ones? Reply from Priya: New ones, they are already ordered and should arrive before we do. Reply from Devon: Great, thanks. Reply from Sam: Sorry to be late to this, but is there parking? Reply from Priya: Limited, and it is first come first served, but there is a public car park two minutes away. Reply from Sam: Understood, thank you. My question is: on what date is the office move happening?

I am going to paste in the terms and conditions of my gym membership and then ask you one small thing. The membership runs on a rolling monthly basis and renews automatically on the first of each month unless cancelled. Cancellation requires thirty days written notice, submitted either in person at the front desk or by email to the address listed on our website. Members may freeze their membership for up to three months in any twelve month period, and a freeze must also be requested with fourteen days notice. Access to the swimming pool is included in the premium tier only, and the standard tier covers the gym floor and the studio classes but not the pool or the sauna. Guest passes are available at a rate of ten pounds per visit, limited to two guests per member per month. Personal training sessions are charged separately and are not covered by any tier of membership. The gym reserves the right to close facilities for maintenance with reasonable notice. Lockers are available on a daily basis only and any items left overnight will be removed. Members must be aged sixteen or over, and members under eighteen require a parent or guardian to countersign the agreement. My question: how many days notice do I need to give to cancel?

The following is a transcript of a short podcast segment about houseplants. Host: So today we are talking about the plants that are genuinely hard to kill, because I think a lot of people come to this feeling like they have a black thumb. Guest: Right, and I always say that is almost never true, it is usually just a mismatch between the plant and the conditions. Host: Give me an example. Guest: Fiddle leaf figs. Everyone wants one because they look wonderful in photographs, and they are genuinely fussy about light and water and being moved. If your first plant is a fiddle leaf fig you will probably conclude you are bad at this. Host: So what should people start with instead? Guest: Pothos, snake plant, ZZ plant. All three tolerate low light, irregular watering, and general neglect. Host: And the snake plant is the one that is sometimes called mother in law's tongue. Guest: That is the one. Host: What about watering, because I think that is where most people go wrong. Guest: Overwatering, almost always. More houseplants die of kindness than of neglect. The rule of thumb is to put a finger in the soil to the second knuckle, and if it is damp, wait. Host: That is good advice. Guest: It is the only advice that matters, honestly. My question about this transcript is: which three plants did the guest recommend for beginners?

Here is a recipe I found and I have one quick question at the end. To make the braised short ribs, begin by patting four pounds of bone-in short ribs completely dry and seasoning them generously with salt and pepper on all sides. Heat two tablespoons of neutral oil in a heavy Dutch oven over medium-high heat until it shimmers, then brown the ribs in batches, about three minutes per side, taking care not to crowd the pan. Transfer the browned ribs to a plate. Lower the heat to medium and add one large onion, two carrots and two ribs of celery, all cut into rough half-inch pieces, and cook until softened and lightly coloured, about eight minutes. Add six cloves of garlic, smashed, and two tablespoons of tomato paste, and cook for another two minutes until the paste darkens. Pour in one bottle of dry red wine and scrape the bottom of the pot thoroughly, then simmer until the wine has reduced by half, roughly ten minutes. Return the ribs to the pot along with four cups of beef stock, four sprigs of thyme and two bay leaves. The liquid should come about three quarters of the way up the ribs. Bring to a bare simmer, cover, and transfer to an oven preheated to three hundred and twenty five degrees Fahrenheit. Braise for three hours, until the meat yields easily to a fork. My question is: what oven temperature does this recipe call for?

I am designing a multi-tenant SaaS platform and I need to decide on a data isolation strategy. The options I am considering are a single shared database with a tenant_id column on every table, a separate schema per tenant within one database, or a fully separate database per tenant. We expect around two thousand tenants in year one, with the largest handful accounting for perhaps forty percent of total data volume. Compliance requirements mean some enterprise customers will demand demonstrable data isolation and the ability to have their data deleted verifiably. We also need to run cross-tenant analytics for our own product decisions, and we want to keep operational overhead manageable with a small team. Migrations are a particular worry, since I have been told that schema-per-tenant becomes painful at scale. Walk me through the trade-offs across cost, operational complexity, blast radius of a bug, compliance defensibility, and migration burden, and then make a concrete recommendation for our situation with reasoning.

Review the following architectural decision and tell me what is wrong with it. We have a payment processing service that writes to a Postgres database, and we want to publish an event to Kafka every time a payment succeeds so that downstream services can react. The current implementation opens a database transaction, inserts the payment row, commits the transaction, and then publishes to Kafka. If the Kafka publish fails we log an error and continue, on the grounds that the payment itself succeeded and we do not want to fail the customer's request over a messaging problem. We have a nightly reconciliation job that compares payment rows against Kafka topic contents and republishes anything missing. My colleague argues this is fine because the reconciliation job catches everything eventually. I am less sure. Explain the failure modes, name the pattern that solves this properly, and describe how you would implement it.

Here is a function from our codebase that has caused two production incidents and I want a thorough review. It accepts a list of user records, deduplicates them by email address, enriches each with data from a third-party API using a thread pool of twenty workers, writes the results to the database in a single transaction, and returns a summary dictionary. There is no timeout on the API calls, exceptions inside worker threads are caught and logged but not re-raised, the deduplication is case-sensitive on email, and the transaction is held open for the entire duration of the enrichment. The function is called from a web request handler with a thirty second timeout. Identify every problem you can see, rank them by severity, and explain how you would restructure it.

Explain the CAP theorem carefully, including what each of consistency, availability and partition tolerance actually mean in the formal statement, why the common phrasing 'pick two' is misleading, how PACELC extends it, and what all of this means practically for someone choosing between Postgres with synchronous replication, DynamoDB, and Cassandra for a system that must stay available during a regional network partition but also must never show a user a stale account balance.

I have a machine learning model in production whose accuracy has degraded from 94% to 81% over six months. The training pipeline has not changed and the model artefact is byte-identical to what we deployed. Input volume has roughly doubled and we onboarded three large customers in a new industry vertical during that period. Our monitoring tracks prediction latency and error rates but not input distributions. Diagnose the likely causes, explain the distinction between the different kinds of drift and which one this most likely is, describe what I should have been monitoring, and lay out a concrete plan to both diagnose the current situation and prevent recurrence.

Summarise the main arguments for and against a four-day working week, covering productivity evidence, effects on employee wellbeing, sector-specific feasibility, and the objections most commonly raised by employers. Aim for around four hundred words.
